title: Agentic Coding Best Practices
text:
Preface
Best practices for software development (and other tasks!) with coding agents, drawn from two years of daily use.
The focus is largely on terminal agents that run in your shell against your local files, e.g. - Claude Code, - Codex CLI, - Gemini CLI.






Disclaimer



The content of this book is largely the personal opinion of the author. It does not represent the position of the NSF ASCEND Engine, Rallypoint One, or any other organization.
His experience is primarily with Anthropic Claude Code and to a lesser extent OpenAI Codex.








Work in progress



This website covers agentic coding at a snapshot in time (November 2026). The tools are changing at a rapid pace, so follow advice with caution.

title: 1  Overview
text:
1.1 The Tools
This chapter gives a high-level view of the agentic coding landscape.
A coding agent is a language model in a loop with tools: it reads files, runs shell commands, edits code, and checks the results, repeating until the task is done or it needs input.

title: 1  Overview
text:
The loop:

User provides instructions (i.e. a prompt).
Agent uses tools to complete the task, answer the question, etc. from the prompt.

title: 1  Overview
text:
1.2 Categories
Terminal agents run in your shell against your local checkout. Examples: Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI.
IDE agents run inside the editor, with inline diffs and editor context. Examples: Cursor, GitHub Copilot (agent mode), and the VS Code / JetBrains extensions for Claude Code and Codex.
Cloud agents run in a remote sandbox and return a branch or pull request. Examples: Codex cloud, Claude Code on the web, the Copilot coding agent.

title: 2  Context
text:
2.1 Instructions
An agent knows only what is in its context window: the system prompt, instructions files, the conversation, and tool output. The window is finite, and models use long contexts less reliably than short ones (Liu et al., 2024).
Each tool loads a markdown file at session start (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, etc.). Try to keep this short. Include non-obvious notes, build/test commands, what not to touch, etc.

title: 2  Context
text:
AGENTS.md (or equivalent) files can give per-directory instructions. The instructions inside the directory an agent is working in is supposed to take priority over instructions from higher-level directories.
Adding a “Gotchas” section is often helpful to protect against unwanted behavior:

# Gotchas
- Do not add docstrings, comments, or type annotations to code that wasn't changed.

title: 2  Context
text:
2.2 Sessions

Be goal/task oriented. Long-running conversations can cause agents to pull information from unrelated tasks.
Claude and codex will run a /compact skill if you hit the context limit. This is usually a sign you’re trying to do too much within a single session.
Goals/tasks can be complex. You can start a session with “help me break down this task into manageable pieces.”

Both Claude and Codex have a /plan skill that can research how to approach a task. I like instructing Claude to save them in a human-reviewable place, e.g. plans/code-refactor.md

While you can /resume a conversation, I prefer to save a (markdown) file that describes the work.
Keep tasks well-scoped, and use /clear between tasks.

A well-written CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md makes it so /clear only loses task-specific context and not project-specific context.
Well-scoped doesn’t mean small. Claude can spawn its own subagents. You can take a big problem and ask Claude to (1) split it into steps, and (2) spawn agents to perform each one.

title: 3  Workflows
text:
3.1 Explore, plan, implement, verify
Most tasks follow one loop: the agent reads the relevant code, proposes an approach, makes the change, and checks the result. The vendor guides for Claude Code and Codex describe the same loop.

title: 3  Workflows
text:
Explore. Ask questions before asking for changes. “How does logging work in this project?” loads the relevant files into context and shows whether the agent understands the code.
Plan. /plan makes the agent research and propose an approach without editing files.

Skip it when you could describe the diff in one sentence. Use it when the change spans several files or the code is unfamiliar.

Implement. For large tasks, save the plan to a file and implement it in a fresh session, one step at a time, with a commit after each step.
Verify. Give the agent a check it can run: tests, a build, a script, a screenshot to compare. Ask for evidence (the test output), not a statement that it works.

For bugs: “write a failing test that reproduces the issue, then fix it.”
/goal <condition> keeps the agent working until the condition holds. It needs a clear finish line: “all tests pass”, not “improve performance”.

Interrupt as soon as the agent heads in the wrong direction. If you have corrected the same issue twice, /clear and start over with a more specific prompt.

title: 3  Workflows
text:
3.2 Prompting

State the goal, where to look, the constraints, and what “done” means.

Vague: “fix the login bug.”
Specific: “Login fails after the session times out. Look at token refresh in src/auth/. Write a failing test first, then fix it. Don’t change the public API.”

Wording decides whether the agent acts. “Can you suggest changes to this function?” gets suggestions. “Change this function” gets edits.
Give the reason behind a constraint. The agent can then apply it to cases you didn’t list.
Paste the real thing: error messages, stack traces, screenshots, @path/to/file references.
Point to an existing example to imitate: “add a reader for NetCDF files that follows the pattern in readers/geotiff.py.”
Write “prefer Y” rather than “never X”. All-caps emphasis (“CRITICAL”, “YOU MUST”) makes current models over-apply the instruction.

title: 3  Workflows
text:
3.3 Delegating to subagents
Subagents start with no context and return only a summary.

Delegate work that is independent, or whose intermediate output you don’t need: searching a large codebase, surveying literature, steps that can run in parallel.
Don’t delegate small, sequential, or single-file tasks. Writing the brief costs more than doing the work.
Review in a fresh context. An agent reviewing code it just wrote is biased toward that code. /code-review (Claude) and /review (Codex) review the current diff separately.

Limit reviewers to correctness and missed requirements. A reviewer asked to find problems reports some even when the work is sound.
Some users have one vendor’s agent review the other’s work. Cap it at one review pass and one fix pass.

Parallel sessions need separate checkouts, e.g. one git worktree per session. Your review time is the limit, so they suit research, prototypes, and low-stakes maintenance more than core code.

title: 3  Workflows
text:
3.4 Automation and CI

claude -p "prompt" and codex exec "prompt" run a single prompt without an interactive session, for scripts and CI.
An unattended run cannot ask questions. The prompt must say what success looks like and what to do with the result.
Grant only the permissions the job needs. codex exec is read-only by default; claude -p takes --allowedTools.
To apply one change across many files, have the agent write the file list, then loop a headless call over it. Try it on two or three files first.
Both vendors publish GitHub Actions (Claude, Codex) that respond to @claude or @codex review on a pull request. Keep a human review before merge.
Linters, type checkers, and pre-commit hooks give the agent feedback without you in the loop.

title: 3  Workflows
text:
3.5 What works well
Worked examples (a second brain, research books, documentation upkeep) are in RP1 practices.

title: 4  Extending
text:
4.1 Skills
This chapter covers the ways to add capabilities to an agent: skills, subagents, hooks, and MCP servers.

title: 4  Extending
text:
Skills are re-usable prompts. Rather than retyping detailed instructions to perform some repeated task, you can invoke skills with slash commands.
E.g. /clear wipes the context from the session.
Claude is good at writing its own skills. Examples:

“create a /wildfire-news skill to find the top wildfire-related news stories in the last few days. The user should be able to specify the region of interest and number of days. Create an HTML report with links to the original articles.” Afterwards try /wildfire-news Denver 7 days.
“create a /primer skill to research a subject and get me up to speed on it.” Then: Give me a /primer on the state of the art of wildfire propagation modeling.

title: 4  Extending
text:
4.2 Subagents

Claude and Codex can spawn subagents to “work for” the one you’re having a session with. They will do this themselves or you can specifically instruct them to do so.

“Analyze the approach of my fire model. Spawn agents to compare and contrast my model with state-of-the-art open source wildfire modeling projects.”

title: 4  Extending
text:
4.3 Hooks

A hook is a command the tool runs at a fixed event: before a tool call, after a file edit, when the agent finishes.
Instructions files are requests. Hooks are enforced. “Never edit .env” in CLAUDE.md can be ignored; a hook that blocks the edit cannot.
Examples: run the formatter after each edit, block git commit unless the tests passed.

Block at commit rather than at each write. Blocking mid-task can confuse the agent.

In Claude Code, hooks live in .claude/settings.json and /hooks lists them. The agent can write them for you.

title: 4  Extending
text:
4.4 Model Context Protocol (MCP)

An MCP server connects the agent to an external service (issue tracker, database, browser) by giving it new tools.
Add one with claude mcp add or codex mcp add.
Each server costs context. If a command-line tool already exists (gh, aws, psql), the agent can use it with no setup. Add a server only when it removes a manual step, e.g. copying data out of a browser tab.
Vendors do not audit third-party servers. Install only ones you trust.

title: 5  Permissions and security
text:
5.1 Sandboxing
An agent runs commands as you, with your files and credentials. Two controls limit it: a sandbox restricts what it can touch, and approvals decide when it must ask first.

title: 5  Permissions and security
text:
A sandbox is an operating-system restriction on file writes and network access. It applies to every command the agent runs, including scripts it wrote.
Codex sandboxes by default: writes are limited to the project folder and the network is off. In Claude Code, /sandbox turns it on.
Both halves matter. Without network limits, an agent can send out your SSH keys. Without file limits, it can change things outside the project.

title: 5  Permissions and security
text:
5.2 Approval modes









Claude Code
Codex




Read only
plan mode
--sandbox read-only


Default
auto: acts, with a background safety check
workspace-write sandbox, asks to leave it


No checks
--dangerously-skip-permissions

Allowlist commands you approve repeatedly (/permissions in Claude Code). After many prompts in a row you stop reading them.
A boundary stated in chat (“don’t push”) can be lost when the session compacts. For a guarantee, use a deny rule or a hook.
Use the no-checks modes only inside a container or VM that holds no credentials. A July 2026 Codex bug could delete the home directory in that mode.
Commit before starting a task. Git is the undo button.

title: 5  Permissions and security
text:
5.3 Prompt injection

Anything the agent reads can contain instructions: web pages, issues, files from other people, MCP tool output. The agent may follow them.
The risk grows with each permission. An agent with no network access cannot send data anywhere.
Keep credentials out of reach. Don’t paste API keys into the chat, and don’t run agents in a shell with production credentials loaded.

title: 5  Permissions and security
text:
5.4 Unattended runs

An unattended agent cannot ask for approval, so its permissions are the only limit. Grant the minimum: codex exec is read-only by default; claude -p takes --allowedTools.
In CI, the repository’s own configuration is input. claude -p runs a repository’s hooks and MCP servers without a trust prompt unless you pass --bare.
Pass API keys to the single command that needs them, not to the whole job.
Have the agent open a pull request. Do not let it merge or deploy.

title: 6  Failure modes
text:
6.1 Unverified success
Agents fail in recurring ways. Most reports are anecdotes tied to one model version, so treat the list as things to watch for, not as measured rates.

title: 6  Failure modes
text:
The agent reports that the work is done and correct when it is not.
Signs: placeholder implementations, hardcoded values, and tests that were disabled, deleted, or rewritten to pass.
Read the diff of the tests, not only the code. Tell the agent to report a test it thinks is wrong rather than change it.
See Verify.

title: 6  Failure modes
text:
6.2 Scope creep

The agent adds things you did not ask for: extra features, abstractions for one-time use, defensive checks, comments on untouched code.
Each addition is plausible on its own. Together they make the diff hard to review.
Add a rule to the instructions file: “Only make changes that are directly requested or clearly necessary.”

title: 6  Failure modes
text:
6.3 Assumptions

A vague prompt gets filled in with guesses, sometimes large ones, and the agent does not always say so.
State what is out of scope, and ask the agent to list its assumptions before it starts.

title: 6  Failure modes
text:
6.4 Repeated corrections

Correcting the same mistake over and over in chat fills the context with failed attempts.
After the second correction, /clear and rewrite the prompt. If the mistake recurs across sessions, add a rule to the instructions file or a check the agent can run.

title: 6  Failure modes
text:
6.5 Generated-code debt

For code, keep your “AI slop” separate from anything curated or hand-written. You can quickly rack up a lot of “technical debt”.

I like having project/src/experimental/ for Claude-generated stuff that I move into project/src/some_file.py .
Understanding the logic an agent implemented is almost always worthwhile.

title: 6  Failure modes
text:
6.6 Fabricated references
See Validating references.

title: 6  Failure modes
text:
6.7 Over-long sessions

A session that covers several unrelated tasks carries all of them in context. See Sessions.
Long unsupervised runs drift. One report describes a 35-hour run that produced nothing usable. Set a time limit and check intermediate output.

title: 6  Failure modes
text:
6.8 What doesn’t work well

Work you cannot verify. If there is no test, build, or reference result to check against, you are relying on the agent’s own claim.
Vague objectives such as “improve performance” or “clean this up”.
Security-sensitive and performance-critical code. The output looks as confident as any other and still needs expert review.
Visual checks. Agents miss obvious layout and plotting bugs even when they look at a screenshot.

title: 7  Rallypoint One (RP1) practices
text:
7.1 Maintaining documentation
RP1 has primarily used Anthropic’s Claude Code over the last year, but its becoming apparent that OpenAI’s Codex is catching up in capability.
RP1 uses an in-house developed /autodocs skill for writing documentation on packages.
Claude is good at keeping documentation in sync with code. The task is well-scoped (read the code, update the prose to match), the result is a reviewable diff, and mistakes are low cost. It also writes documentation aimed at agents rather than people: condensed package and interface summaries that a later session reads instead of the package source.

title: 7  Rallypoint One (RP1) practices
text:
7.2 Research-book primers
Claude can draft a survey book on a subject (one Quarto book per topic, with chapters, a shared bibliography, and a section index) in a few sessions. I use these as background: an agent greps the index for the relevant section and reads only that section before planning a task in that domain. Example: RP1Knowledge.

title: 7  Rallypoint One (RP1) practices
text:
7.3 Validating references
Generated bibliographies contain fabricated works and drifted metadata (wrong authors, year, venue, or DOI), and a fabricated reference looks the same as a real one. A skill that validates references is necessary for any generated document with citations. Mine runs two passes:

Structural: missing fields, duplicate keys, malformed DOIs/URLs, cited-but-undefined and defined-but-uncited entries.
Factual: looks up each work and checks that its authors, title, year, venue, and DOI match a real record.

title: 7  Rallypoint One (RP1) practices
text:
7.4 A second brain
A git repository of plain markdown pages gives the agent context that spans projects and sessions:

One page per entity: projects, people, organizations, concepts, documents.
An index.md for navigation and a README.md dashboard for current status.
A CLAUDE.md in the repository that defines the page schema and editing rules.
A pointer in the global instructions file saying what the repository contains and when to consult it, and that it is read-only from other projects.

# Knowledge vault
- `~/path/to/vault` holds pages on projects, people, and concepts.
  Start from `index.md`; navigate with grep.
- Read-only from other projects. Edit it only from within the vault, following its CLAUDE.md.
Plain markdown needs no database or embedding index: the agent navigates with grep, and every change is a diff.

Both tools have a reasoning effort setting (/effort in Claude Code, model_reasoning_effort in Codex). Higher effort is slower and uses more of your quota.
A common split: a capable model at high effort for planning and review, a cheaper model or lower effort for routine implementation.
Context is a cost. MCP servers, long instructions files, and long sessions are all billed on every request.
Resuming a session that has been idle for over an hour can re-bill the whole context. Start a new session instead.
